The moment that global investors focused on AI computing power have been awaiting is imminent. Since OpenAI's ChatGPT swept the globe and triggered an unprecedented wave of artificial intelligence investment, Wall Street institutional investors and retail investors worldwide have been anticipating this event every quarter: the release of the second-quarter earnings report by NVIDIA (NVDA.US), regarded as the world's most important stock and the "supreme dominator" of AI chips. Other major technology companies, including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Tesla—collectively known as the "Magnificent Seven"—reported their earnings nearly a month ago. NVIDIA is finally set to disclose its detailed second-quarter financial results and its outlook for future quarters. The so-called "Magnificent Seven" (Mag 7), which hold substantial weight (over 40%) in both the S&P 500 Index and the Nasdaq 100 Index, include NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft, Google, Tesla, Amazon, and Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook. They are the core drivers behind the S&P 500 Index's repeated record highs and are regarded by top Wall Street investment institutions as the portfolio most capable of delivering substantial returns to investors against the backdrop of the largest technological transformation since the internet era. The S&P 500 Index has surged by over $3 trillion in cumulative gains during the past three years, driven largely by an "AI super bull market." This rally has been primarily fueled by tech giants viewed as the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom—the seven largest U.S. technology companies (the "Magnificent Seven"). It has also been strongly propelled by chipmakers that have significantly benefited from massive global investments in AI computing infrastructure, such as SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, Micron, Taiwan Semiconductor, and Broadcom; the three major storage product manufacturers (SanDisk, Western Digital, and Seagate); and power system suppliers like Constellation Energy. Zhitong Finance APP observes that, as NVIDIA prepares to release its earnings, global chip stocks—particularly semiconductor shares closely tied to the AI computing theme—have struggled to sustain their rebound since August and over the past month, following a sharp decline in July. Market concerns have resurfaced regarding whether global enterprises can achieve robust returns from their immense investments in artificial intelligence. Consequently, investors are eager to learn whether enterprise demand for NVIDIA's next-generation AI computing cluster, Vera-Rubin, will prove stronger than that for the Blackwell architecture, amid expanding demand for AI applications. Additionally, they seek insight into how NVIDIA's management, including Jensen Huang, views the revenue prospects for both B-side and C-side AI applications in the future. Strong growth data from the cloud computing businesses of Microsoft, Amazon, and Google has helped alleviate some investor concerns. However, rising AI infrastructure spending by Google and Meta Platforms has also caused unease among investors. NVIDIA's upcoming second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings report has evolved from a mere "chip leader earnings release" into a systemic stress test for the global AI capital expenditure cycle. Wall Street consensus expects revenue of approximately $92 billion and adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.09, with data center revenue projected to reach a staggering $85.4 billion, representing a 107% year-over-year increase. However, Jefferies, a major Wall Street financial institution, has raised the "true bullish threshold" to $95 billion for the second quarter and approximately $108 billion for the next fiscal quarter. The options market is pricing in two-way volatility of about 6%–7%, corresponding to a market capitalization change of over $320 billion. Notably, NVIDIA's stock fell the day after each of its previous four consecutive strong beats on earnings and guidance, indicating that simply surpassing market consensus is no longer sufficient to drive a new surge in the AI computing supply chain. $92 Billion "Computing Power Exam"! NVIDIA Earnings Become the Master Switch for AI Trading According to consensus analyst expectations compiled by institutions, NVIDIA is projected to achieve an adjusted EPS of $2.09 and revenue of approximately $92 billion in the second quarter. This implies a 96% year-over-year jump in total revenue and continues to show an accelerating growth trajectory against a high base on a quarter-over-quarter basis. In the previous quarter, NVIDIA updated its financial reporting framework, breaking down data center revenue into sales to hyperscale cloud service providers (Hyperscalers) such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon, and sales to AI Cloud, Industrial, and Enterprise customers (ACIE). Revenue from personal computers, gaming consoles, workstations, robotics, and automotive businesses is now consolidated under NVIDIA's edge computing segment. Based on Wall Street consensus expectations, NVIDIA's data center revenue for the second fiscal quarter is projected to exceed $85.4 billion, implying a substantial 107% year-over-year growth. Revenue from hyperscale cloud service providers is expected to reach $43.5 billion, while ACIE sales are forecast at $41.7 billion. The majority of NVIDIA's revenue continues to come from hyperscale cloud service providers such as Amazon, Google, and Microsoft. However, these global leaders in cloud computing are all developing their own AI chips and server CPUs to reduce their reliance on NVIDIA's computing infrastructure. Some have even begun focusing on selling AI computing clusters based on their proprietary chips to large third-party customers, which could pose a long-term relative disadvantage for NVIDIA in the future. NVIDIA continues to sign cooperation agreements with numerous technology and financial enterprises within the artificial intelligence ecosystem. Earlier this month, the leading AI chipmaker made a major announcement that it is collaborating with BlackRock, Blackstone, KKR, Apollo, Brookfield, and Goldman Sachs to establish a $500 billion capital pool, a move that will facilitate the securitization of large-scale NVIDIA AI GPU assets. NVIDIA recently stated that it would support SB Energy and OpenAI in constructing a massive 8-gigawatt data center in Ohio, with investment amounts reaching up to $150 billion. NVIDIA is partnering with BlackRock, Blackstone, KKR, Apollo, Brookfield, and Goldman Sachs to establish a $500 billion capital pool and supporting SB Energy and OpenAI in building an 8-gigawatt data center with investments of up to $150 billion. These developments indicate that NVIDIA's long-standing GPU-centric growth model is evolving from simple GPU sales into a full-stack AI ecosystem comprising 'AI chips + high-performance network infrastructure + an AI application developer ecosystem centered around CUDA and NVIDIA's open-source large models + long-term capital.' In particular, NVIDIA appears to be increasingly focused on reducing clients' upfront capital pressure for AI computing power through GPU securitization and project financing, aiming to transform large orders for AI chips or AI computing clusters into financeable, leasable long-term computing assets. However, this also binds NVIDIA more deeply to client utilization rates, AI application monetization, and debt servicing capabilities. If revenue growth from AI inference fails to cover the high costs of computing power, commitments to ecosystem financing and GPU residual values could become new channels for risk transmission. Is a $5 trillion market cap far from NVIDIA's endpoint? High growth meets high expectations in a direct collision. NVIDIA's current market capitalization is approximately $5.25 trillion, significantly higher than second-place Apple, which stands at around $4.5 trillion. However, some analysts bullish on NVIDIA's stock price outlook believe the gap between the two will widen rapidly, starting with NVIDIA's release of its second-quarter earnings after market close on August 26 (Eastern Time). The expectations facing NVIDIA before its earnings releases this year have not been exceptionally high. In both 2024 and 2025, the expected P/E ratio prior to the second-quarter earnings announcement was approximately 35x. For most of this year, the forward P/E ratio has remained at a relatively attractive level of around 24x. Based on a market capitalization of $5.25 trillion, NVIDIA needs only a roughly 14% increase to surpass the $6 trillion mark; if the expected P/E ratio rises to a relatively optimistic 35x, the theoretical upside is approximately 46%, corresponding to a market capitalization of about $7.65 trillion. This judgment is supported by the ongoing expansion of AI infrastructure construction, the continued doubling of data center revenue, and NVIDIA's systemic advantages in GPUs, high-performance Ethernet networking, and the AI software developer ecosystem. However, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are accelerating the deployment of self-developed ASICs/XPUs, and the return on investment for AI spending has become a key focus of market scrutiny. Therefore, this earnings report could either serve as the starting gun for a renewed acceleration in AI trading or become a milestone watershed moment where valuations shift from 'near-infinite demand for computing power' to 'verification of sustainable cash flow growth across the entire AI ecosystem.' If NVIDIA's earnings and future outlook significantly exceed market expectations, particularly by demonstrating demand for Vera-Rubin far surpassing consensus forecasts—for instance, if orders for Vera-Rubin over the next two years are projected to exceed $1 trillion—the forward P/E ratio could rise to a relatively optimistic 35x. This would trigger a substantial surge in NVIDIA's stock price, driving its market capitalization beyond $6 trillion by the end of 2026. Based on NVIDIA's current market capitalization of $5.25 trillion, a 46% increase in share price would actually push the company's valuation to $7.65 trillion—far exceeding the consensus expectations of Wall Street analysts covering the stock. Since NVIDIA needs only a 14% rise to reach the $6 trillion mark, some analysts consider it highly probable that the company will achieve this milestone shortly after its earnings release. This makes the stock currently very attractive; even if its valuation multiple does not revert to historical norms, 2027 is still expected to be a strong year for the stock, as its valuation entering 2027 will be relatively low given its robust earnings growth trajectory. If NVIDIA reports quarterly results that significantly exceed expectations and provides strong guidance for the third quarter, it could spark a rally in its stock price, pushing NVIDIA back to the valuation levels it typically commands at this time of year—approximately 35 times forward earnings. If NVIDIA achieves this, its market capitalization will rise to heights never before reached by any company. For NVIDIA, beating expectations has become the norm. In Q4 of fiscal 2026, management guided revenue at $65 billion, but the company ultimately reported $68 billion. In Q1 of fiscal 2027, management provided guidance of $78 billion, yet NVIDIA generated actual revenue of $82 billion. Such outperformance has become embedded in market expectations. While management has guided Q2 revenue to $91 billion, most investors anticipate actual results of at least $92 billion. Meanwhile, Wall Street institutions such as Jefferies have issued even higher estimates of $95 billion or more. For investors applying stricter benchmarks, noting that revenue in the second quarter of the previous fiscal year was $46.7 billion, NVIDIA would need to achieve $93.4 billion in Q2 of fiscal 2027 to realize a year-on-year doubling. As Rubin prepares to succeed Blackwell, will NVIDIA's earnings report ignite a new primary uptrend in the AI computing power theme? Using a unified baseline of a closing price of $214.72 on August 21, approximately 24.22 billion shares outstanding, and a market capitalization of $5.20 trillion, 59 Wall Street analysts maintain a consensus "Strong Buy" rating for NVIDIA, with an average 12-month target price of $304.73. This implies a potential upside of approximately 41.92%, corresponding to a market capitalization of about $7.38 trillion, representing a potential increase of roughly $2.18 trillion. The highest target price is $500, set by Baird analyst Tristan Gerra, implying a potential share price appreciation of approximately 132.9% and a corresponding market capitalization of about $12.11 trillion, which is a potential increase of roughly $6.91 trillion from current levels. These market capitalization projections assume the total share count remains largely unchanged. Gerra maintains an "Outperform" rating with a $500 target price, based on the core thesis that NVIDIA is evolving from a GPU supplier into a full-stack AI platform encompassing CUDA, NVLink, AI Enterprise, and rack-level systems. The company continues to gain share in the hyperscale cloud computing and inference markets, and the penetration rate of Vera-Rubin among frontier model companies may exceed that of Blackwell. The standalone Vera CPU is expected to unlock an incremental market of approximately $200 billion due to its performance advantages. Furthermore, agent-driven AI will drive global annual spending on AI infrastructure from over $1 trillion in 2027 to $3–4 trillion by 2030, continuously strengthening NVIDIA's pricing power, revenue related to the AI application development ecosystem, and free cash flow growth. Regarding NVIDIA's upcoming earnings and outlook, the market is primarily focused on the "quality" of demand growth rather than just the "scale of growth." This explains why NVIDIA's stock price has continued to weaken in recent quarters despite strong earnings. Analysts expect hyperscale cloud providers and AI Cloud, Industrial, and Enterprise (ACIE) customers to contribute $43.5 billion and $41.7 billion, respectively. If ACIE continues to grow rapidly, it would indicate that NVIDIA is reducing its reliance on a few key customers like Microsoft, Amazon, and Google, with demand expanding from training clusters to inference, enterprise agents, sovereign AI, and industrial AI. Conversely, if growth remains predominantly driven by capital expenditures from hyperscale cloud giants, the market will grow more concerned about share dilution caused by U.S. tech giants developing their own ASICs/XPUs. Therefore, the most critical operational signals in the earnings report will center on whether the customer base continues to diversify, whether GPU utilization rates remain high, and whether token revenue and cloud business growth demonstrate that computing power procurement is generating real cash flow rather than merely accumulating idle capacity. The second decisive focus is the product transition from Blackwell to Vera-Rubin. Rubin continues the Oberon NVL72 rack form factor, allowing for the reuse of power supply, liquid cooling, cabinet, and manufacturing systems already established for GB200/GB300. If the assembly time for compute trays is reduced from approximately two hours to five minutes, it signifies that NVIDIA is transforming complex AI server projects into modular, scalable deliveries akin to an "AI factory." Jefferies expects VR/R200 to account for approximately 12% of GPU revenue in Q3 of fiscal 2027, exceeding 40% in Q4, and becoming the dominant product in Q1 of fiscal 2028. The Vera CPU integrates CPUs, GPUs, networking, and CUDA software into a rack-level platform through LPDDR5X and NVLink coherent interconnects. If management confirms that Rubin will enter mass production on schedule and accelerate significantly starting in the January quarter next year, the market's valuation anchor may shift from "when Blackwell peaks" to "Rubin initiating the next growth curve." The third new narrative is "open models seeding demand + supply chain locking supply." While Nemotron, Cosmos, GR00T, Alpamayo, NeMo, and the Agent Toolkit may not directly contribute massive model revenue themselves, they channel developer workloads toward CUDA, TensorRT, NIM, DGX, and RTX platforms. Small Language Models (SLMs), in particular, are well-suited for agent tool calls, enterprise-specific tasks, and edge-side inference, helping NVIDIA upgrade from "selling GPUs" to defining the token production environment. Meanwhile, NVIDIA has secured advanced CoWoS-L packaging, HBM, optical components, land, and power through multi-year agreements, essentially controlling the scarcest input factors for AI factories. This means competitors, even with chip designs, may be constrained by packaging yields, memory availability, and delivery lead times. By launching the Nemotron Alliance and collaborating with multiple AI labs to develop open models, NVIDIA further reinforces this hardware-software flywheel. Rising memory costs constitute a "double-edged sword" for the earnings report. Current media reports suggest that complete servers equipped with NVIDIA chips may see price increases of over 15% due to rising costs of memory components such as HBM and DRAM, rather than a uniform 15% price hike for NVIDIA GPUs. These price adjustments cover Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems scheduled for delivery early next year. On one hand, this proves that AI memory, advanced packaging, and complete system capacity remain extremely tight, highlighting the bargaining power of bottleneck suppliers like SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung, and Taiwan Semiconductor. On the other hand, it raises the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) per megawatt for data centers, compresses margins for server contract manufacturers, and strengthens the incentive for cloud providers to use self-developed ASICs for mature inference tasks. Consequently, the market will closely examine whether NVIDIA can fully pass on these costs while maintaining gross margins in the mid-70% range, and continue to offset server price hikes for customers through improvements in performance-per-watt and reductions in cost-per-token. NVIDIA has provided up to approximately $105 billion in credit support for the OpenAI–SB Energy project and participates in a $500 billion GPU financing pool. This arrangement helps alleviate capital constraints faced by customers in a high-interest-rate environment, but it also positions NVIDIA simultaneously as an equipment supplier, an investor, and a credit supporter. If its financial report delivers revenue close to $95 billion, next-quarter guidance near $108 billion, confirms accelerated Rubin development, stable gross margins, and no major delays in power and packaging delivery, while clearly defining responsibilities for leases, power payments, and residual value guarantees, then the trading hotspot around the AI computing theme is likely to extend beyond just NVIDIA’s GPU compute clusters. It could further accelerate its spread across the entire AI computing industry chain—including HBM/DRAM/NAND memory, CoWoS/3D advanced packaging, MLCC/ABF substrates, data center CPUs, high-performance network infrastructure, optical interconnects, liquid cooling, and data center power infrastructure—forming a new super-cycle "main upward wave" at the industry-chain level. If NVIDIA’s earnings and quarterly outlook only slightly exceed expectations, with next-quarter guidance close to $102–$104 billion, or if its financing obligations, gross margins, and Rubin mass-production timeline remain ambiguous, a scenario of "strong earnings but stagnant stock price" with high-level consolidation is more likely to occur. In other words, whether the AI computing industry chain enters a new main upward trend depends not on whether NVIDIA can continue to grow, but on whether it can prove that future growth stems from profitable token demand rather than GPU orders generated through its own credit cycle. title: Michael Burry Says Nvidia Q2 Earnings Will Be 'Lights Out' And '100% Of Announced Revenue Is Circular' - TradingView
content: “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry expects Nvidia (NVDA) to deliver a blowout quarterly result on Wednesday, even as he continues betting against the chipmaker over circular financing, concentrated spending and excessive AI hype. NVDA stock is up 7% so far this month, on track for its best month since April. Nvidia will report its second-quarter results after Wednesday’s closing bell. When asked on Substack about Nvidia’s upcoming earnings and their significance for the semiconductor pullback, Burry replied: “They will be lights out and accompanied by the kind of hype that tells you FOMO has almost all the people that would buy it already in it.” In a separate conversation about Nvidia’s exposure to OpenAI and CoreWeave, Burry said: “At the chip makers, roughly 100% of announced revenue is circular. That’s per the BIS [Bank for International Settlements].” According to Fiscal.ai, Nvidia’s revenue is expected to more than double from a year earlier to $91.48 billion, with adjusted earnings rising to $2.07 per share. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) are projected to more than double to $61.83 billion. Sequentially, revenue is projected to grow nearly 13% to $92.07 billion and adjusted earnings to increase almost 12% to $2.09 per share, and EBITDA is forecast to rise 13% to $61.99 billion, per Koyfin. Burry has repeatedly said chipmakers, cloud providers, and AI companies are increasingly investing in, financing, or guaranteeing business for one another, creating circular flows that can make demand appear stronger and more independent than it is. His thesis also focuses on Nvidia’s reliance on a small group of hyperscale customers, including Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet. Burry argues that a material spending reduction by even one major customer could significantly affect Nvidia’s revenue. In May, he highlighted $182 billion in non-cancellable supply commitments, exceeding Nvidia’s annual operating cash flow. Burry also contends that AI chips lose economic value faster than the accounting depreciation schedules used by hyperscalers and specialized cloud providers suggest. New generations of hardware can quickly make older systems less competitive, potentially limiting customers’ ability to recover their investments. Burry has maintained and expanded his bearish Nvidia positions throughout this year despite expecting strong near-term results. In early June, he adjusted several put positions extending into 2027. Even last month, Burry reiterated concerns about hyperscaler spending, chip depreciation, and the gap between announced and deployed AI capacity. Earlier this month, Burry rolled part of his December 2026 Nvidia puts into June 2027 contracts while maintaining strikes in the low-$100 range. He also added to the December 2026 and June 2027 positions. Wall Street remains mostly bullish, pointing to sustained generative-AI demand, Nvidia’s strong access to chip supply and upcoming product launches. Benchmark expects the October-quarter outlook, early Vera Rubin deployments and gross-margin trajectory to matter more than a modest earnings beat or miss. RBC Capital sees another “strong quarter,” driven by AI demand, the Rubin ramp and a potential 50%-plus increase in average selling prices. Oppenheimer expects Blackwell Ultra, VR200 and potential China accelerator sales to drive further upside. The firms’ price targets imply about 23% to 56% upside from Nvidia’s current market price. Meanwhile, Koyfin’s average target represents about 42% upside. Of the 62 analysts covering Nvidia, 10 rate it ‘Strong Buy,’ 49 recommend ‘Buy,’ two say ‘Hold,’ and one rates it ‘Sell.’ None have a ‘Strong Sell’ rating. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for NVDA has been ‘bearish’ over the past week amid a 3% rise in 24-hour message volumes. One user said, “$NVDA earnings boost next week; we might expect a big surge. Let's buy shares on Monday.” Another user said, “$NVDA earnings last November collapsed the market, expecting the same to happen this week as people hate ai and hate data centers even more.” Nvidia is the best-performing “Magnificent Seven” stock this year, with shares up 15% year to date. title: NVDA Stock Comes Off Rough Week: AI Darling Reportedly Plans Major Price Hike As Q2 Earnings Loom - Stocktwits
content: Nvidia Corp.’s stock gained nearly 1% in overnight trading late Sunday after a challenging week on the market, with trends pointing to a mixed setup ahead of its earnings report on Wednesday. A spate of developments appears to be contributing to the stock’s move. Some of Nvidia’s top customers have been told that prices for systems, including Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell, will rise by more than 15% starting in early 2027, according to a Bloomberg report on Saturday. The source-based report indicated that surging memory prices are likely contributing to the increase. Companies that build the servers under contract for large data center operators such as Microsoft, Google and Oracle have recently notified their customers of the forthcoming increases, according to the report. Nvidia has struck a deal with AI startup Poolside to build open-weight AI models to compete with China's DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing people familiar with the matter. Nvidia will invest $1 billion in the company and pay $6 billion to license Poolside’s technology and hire most of its engineers. The deal will also present a direct challenge to U.S. AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. “Here’s where it gets interesting: Nvidia is now officially competing with frontier companies. Companies they’ve invested hundreds of billions into over the last several years,” Alex Finn, founder of Silicon Valley-based AI startup Henry Intelligent Machines PBC (HIM), posted on X. “On top of that, they’ll have a massive compute advantage because well… they are the compute.” Finn argued that demand for compute is insatiable, open-source AI will play a major role, and companies serious about AI need their own compute infrastructure. Assets tied to compute, energy and the broader AI buildout, he added, will only become more valuable. Meanwhile, Nvidia made a minority investment in Cloverleaf, which works with utilities and energy providers to secure infrastructure for data center sites. NVDA shares have fallen for six consecutive sessions, losing 4.8% in the period. The past week was the worst for the stock in nearly two months, although the company’s market capitalization has stayed above $5 trillion. GOOGL stock was down 0.2% in overnight trading, while MSFT and ORCL were flat. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for NVDA dipped over the past week and was ‘bearish’ as of late Sunday, while message volume dipped 21.4% for the week. “$NVDA Overnight trading starts in 20 minutes. Where are we going? What price will we hit in the first 5-10 minutes of trading tonight? I say $220,” a trader posted, forecasting a 2.5% rise from the stock’s closing price on Friday. On the setup, research firm Bullseye Gains posted on Stocktwits: “$NVDA is primed for a decisive beat-and-raise quarter, setting the stage for what should be management's most bullish conference call in years.” “Supply checks indicate hyperscaler compute spending is accelerating across the board, and recent reporting from The Information highlights that major cloud giants remain completely tethered to Nvidia hardware, with server builders noting 15%+ pricing power resilience on next-gen systems as customers aggressively lock down capacity,” it said, adding that the stock would hit a fresh high in the near term. The price increase “should be a positive for $MU and $SKHY on Monday ($MVLL, $SKHL),” said another trader. The market is gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly results due after the market closes on Wednesday. The AI chipmaker’s earnings have become a closely watched event, with the potential to dictate broader market direction and shape sentiment toward the AI industry as a whole. Wall Street is also expecting another beat-and-raise quarter, as accelerating cloud spending from Microsoft and Amazon and major AI commitments from SpaceX and OpenAI reinforce confidence in demand for Nvidia’s chips. Second-quarter revenue is expected to rise 13% to $92.01 billion, while adjusted profit is seen rising 11% to $2.08 per share, per estimates from Koyfin. Investors will also track Nvidia’s gross margins as high-bandwidth-memory costs rise, along with updates on China sales and the Rubin Ultra roadmap. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) are tracking their best monthly performance since May as the company announced a key pre-flight testing milestone for Neutron’s world-first reusable Hungry Hippo fairing. RKLB stock fell 1% on Friday, marking its fourth consecutive session of losses, but shares are still up 12% for the month. Rocket Lab is now testing whether Hungry Hippo can open and close as intended during a mission. The exercise recreates the fairing’s role in releasing Neutron’s second stage and payload before the reusable first stage heads back to Earth. A fairing is a protective shell that shields a rocket’s payload from heat and aerodynamic forces during launch. “Pre-flight testing with Hungry Hippo is underway,” the company said on X. Hungry Hippo differs from traditional rocket fairings, which are typically discarded or recovered separately. Its two halves stay connected to Neutron’s first stage, opening for about 1.5 seconds before closing to create a single integrated vehicle for the return journey. Once the current campaign concludes, the fairing will be placed back in its hangar until Neutron’s interstage arrives in Virginia for mating. The latest update comes after a qualification and acceptance campaign completed in December. Rocket Lab subjected Hungry Hippo to 275,000 pounds of force to reproduce peak aerodynamic pressure, while testing its control-surface hubs beyond 125% of projected flight loads. The fairing reached Wallops Island, Virginia, in January, where it underwent inspections and received key flight hardware. Earlier this month, Rocket Lab confirmed that thermal protection, control surfaces, avionics and fluid systems had been installed before the vehicle moved outdoors for further checks. CEO Peter Beck said completing those tests would leave Hungry Hippo “essentially finished and ready for launch.” The next steps include joining the fairing with Neutron’s interstage, assembling the broader vehicle and conducting integrated checks, static-fire testing and a wet dress rehearsal. Rocket Lab is still aiming to place Neutron on the launch pad during the fourth quarter of 2026. However, Beck has cautioned that “the window for an end-of-year launch is narrowing.” Neutron is designed to place as much as 13,000 kilograms into orbit. Its nine Archimedes engines are expected to produce a combined 1.45 million pounds of thrust. The medium-lift rocket would expand the missions Rocket Lab can pursue beyond Electron’s small-launch market. Kepler Communications and the U.S. Space Force have already booked dedicated Neutron flights. Last week, Rocket Lab completed Electron’s 93rd flight and 14th mission of 2026, deploying its ninth QPS-SAR satellite for Japan’s iQPS. Nine more dedicated launches are booked through 2030. The company also expanded its national-security business. Viasat selected Rocket Lab’s Lightning-GEO platform for an anti-jam U.S. Space Force communications satellite, while Rocket Lab joined the $981 million-ceiling NITE-STAR program, allowing it to compete for future spacecraft, software and mission-operations work. The developments came as U.S. President Donald Trump unveiled a policy targeting more than 1,000 U.S. launches and reentries annually by 2030 through faster reviews, additional launch sites, priority airspace and streamlined procurement. Bitcoin (BTC) investors need to be careful about using traditional economic data and historical models to predict the direction of U.S. Treasury yields, veteran macro investor Jordi Visser said on Sunday. Visser said governments are increasingly willing to intervene in markets to keep borrowing costs in check. “They’re saying they don’t want yields to go higher because we have a debt and deficit problem,” Visser said, adding that betting against government intervention is “a very, very, very dangerous game.” Speaking on Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's decision to double long-end buyback capacity, Visser said, “He's leaning on the Fed because you see multiple storyboards going on, you have to be careful. At best, he says he's a political actor. He's focused on the midterm. This is all noise, guys. This is just stuff going on.” Visser said traditional businesses are facing more pressure as AI speeds up competition and destroys the growth assumptions that investors use to value them. Crypto is minor compared to traditional equities markets, he said, but it might grow much quicker since it would provide the financial “guardrails” for the new AI-driven economy. He also rejected persistent pessimistic macro narratives on higher rates, rising long-term yields, debt and deficits, saying investors frequently fall into an “end-game bias” by assuming those outcomes are inevitable. Visser said AI-driven competition is shortening the window investors have to appraise companies and making long-term discounted-cash-flow assumptions less dependable. The speed of technology development is altering company models and growth expectations, he said, making it hard for investors to price many public businesses with confidence three years out. At the same time, he noted the S&P 500’s (SPX) profit growth remains robust, although valuation multiples are under pressure from rising competition. Visser is especially bullish on Bitcoin as the AI-driven digital economy grows. Bitcoin is “basically the S&P 500 of the crypto world,” he said, adding that it might become the leading store of value in the digital economy. He also stated he had pared back some of his AI-trade exposure and moved money into Bitcoin and silver, while keeping some AI-infrastructure bets intact. Visser also sees an upside for Ethereum (ETH), saying the overall crypto ecosystem may eventually overtake Bitcoin. He thinks Ethereum should outperform because the investment thesis is more and more about the ecosystem and the applications that are being built around crypto and not just Bitcoin, he added. Nvidia (NasdaqGS: NVDA) has agreed a reported US$7b Poolside AI licensing deal that combines a non exclusive technology license, investment and key hires. The structure uses licensing plus hiring Poolside AI employees instead of a full acquisition, which can attract more regulatory scrutiny. The agreement is intended to give Nvidia greater control over industrial scale AI model capacity while keeping Poolside AI independent. Investors are watching whether this template becomes a repeatable way for large tech companies to expand AI capabilities without traditional M&A. Nvidia is far from the only company tied to the build out of AI infrastructure, so it can be useful to compare this news with a broader group of stocks exposed to similar demand trends through 55 AI infrastructure stocks. NVIDIA operates as a data center scale AI infrastructure company across the US, Europe and Asia, so deals like this are closely tied to its role in supplying computing power for large AI models. For you as an investor, it highlights how NVIDIA is working to deepen its ecosystem beyond the sale of chips alone. 4 things going right for NVIDIA that this headline doesn't cover. The central bet in Nvidia's Narrative is that AI demand and full stack offerings will keep deepening customer reliance on its platform. This US$7b Poolside AI licensing structure speaks directly to that story, because it targets control of AI model capacity without relying on classic acquisitions. "The company is capturing a growing share of the expanding value chain by deploying full stack AI infrastructure, deepening customer lock in, boosting recurring software revenues, and supporting high gross margins..." Read the full NVIDIA narrative to see the case behind these numbers For that thesis, the Poolside deal clearly supports the catalyst that Nvidia can shift from pure GPU supplier to wider AI infrastructure partner. By licensing Model Factory technology, investing US$1b and hiring key staff while Poolside stays independent, Nvidia strengthens its software and services layer that sits on top of its chips and networking. At the same time, this structure puts pressure on a different part of the Narrative, which flags rising costs and ecosystem risks as Nvidia pushes further into AI factories. Large off balance sheet style commitments and aggressive talent hiring can increase complexity, especially as rivals like AMD and Broadcom also chase AI platform roles and customers weigh custom silicon options.
